Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have become an essential infrastructure for Artificial General
Intelligence (AGI), yet their lack of well-defined memory management systems hinders the devel-
opment of long-context reasoning, continual personalization, and knowledge consistency.Existing
models mainly rely on static parameters and short-lived contextual states, limiting their ability to
track user preferences or update knowledge over extended periods.While Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG) introduces external knowledge in plain text, it remains a stateless workaround
without lifecycle control or integration with persistent representations.Recent work has modeled the
training and inference cost of LLMs from a memory hierarchy perspective, showing that introducing
an explicit memory layer between parameter memory and external retrieval can substantially
reduce these costs by externalizing specific knowledge [1]. Beyond computational efficiency, LLMs
face broader challenges arising from how information is distributed over time and context, requiring
systems capable of managing heterogeneous knowledge spanning different temporal scales and
sources. To address this challenge, we propose MemOS, a memory operating system that treats
memory as a manageable system resource. It unifies the representation, scheduling, and evolution
of plaintext, activation-based, and parameter-level memories, enabling cost-efficient storage and
retrieval. As the basic unit, a MemCube encapsulates both memory content and metadata such as
provenance and versioning. MemCubes can be composed, migrated, and fused over time, enabling
flexible transitions between memory types and bridging retrieval with parameter-based learning.
MemOS establishes a memory-centric system framework that brings controllability, plasticity, and
evolvability to LLMs, laying the foundation for continual learning and personalized modeling.

Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have become an essential infrastructure for Artificial General
Intelligence (AGI), yet their lack of well-defined memory management systems hinders the devel-
opment of long-context reasoning, continual personalization, and knowledge consistency.Existing
models mainly rely on static parameters and short-lived contextual states, limiting their ability to
track user preferences or update knowledge over extended periods.While Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG) introduces external knowledge in plain text, it remains a stateless workaround
without lifecycle control or integration with persistent representations.Recent work has modeled the
training and inference cost of LLMs from a memory hierarchy perspective, showing that introducing
an explicit memory layer between parameter memory and external retrieval can substantially
reduce these costs by externalizing specific knowledge [1]. Beyond computational efficiency, LLMs
face broader challenges arising from how information is distributed over time and context, requiring
systems capable of managing heterogeneous knowledge spanning different temporal scales and
sources. To address this challenge, we propose MemOS, a memory operating system that treats
memory as a manageable system resource. It unifies the representation, scheduling, and evolution
of plaintext, activation-based, and parameter-level memories, enabling cost-efficient storage and
retrieval. As the basic unit, a MemCube encapsulates both memory content and metadata such as
provenance and versioning. MemCubes can be composed, migrated, and fused over time, enabling
flexible transitions between memory types and bridging retrieval with parameter-based learning.
MemOS establishes a memory-centric system framework that brings controllability, plasticity, and
evolvability to LLMs, laying the foundation for continual learning and personalized modeling.

Whenever a builder starts constructing a house, the most important work happens where
no one can see. Before the walls go up, and long before the paint dries, the builder has to dig down

the most beautiful house will come crashing down the moment a heavy storm hits.

We are constantly taught to look successful, keep our social media feeds bright, and pretend that
our lives are completely put together. But behind those bright smiles, many of our youth are quietly
struggling. There is the heavy stress of exams, the search for stable jobs, the ache of loneliness
in distant cities and hostels, and the fear of falling behind. In Matthew 7, Jesus does not care about
the paint on our walls. He looks straight through the appearance and asks one vital question: what
is holding your life up from beneath?

Jesus warns us that simply saying “Lord, Lord” is never enough. It is easy to come to
church every Sunday, wear nice clothes, sing the songs, and still be building our lives on loose
sand. Sand is comfortable because it requires zero effort. It means living for instant likes, following
the crowd, and treating God like an afterthought.
Building on the rock takes real work. It means choosing to dig past our pride and our selfish
desires. To be rooted in Christ means our worth is not decided by our job title, our salary, or what
people say about us. It means making time every day to pray, read His Word, and anchor our
identity in the love of Jesus. When your roots grip the bedrock of Christ, no trend or hardship can
wash you away.

Both builders in the parable heard the exact same words of Jesus. The only difference was
that one walked away and did nothing, while the other went home and put those words into practice.
Real faith is never just sitting quietly in a pew. Faith has hands and feet.
In our Mar Thoma tradition, faith is always meant to be lived out. When we are driven by
faith, our belief changes how we act on Monday morning. It means being honest in an office where
others cheat. It means standing up for a friend who is left out. It means trusting God with your
future even when the doors seem closed. Faith does not keep the rain away, but it gives us the
courage to keep walking through the downpour.
This question remains before us as followers of Christ. Can you join the sorrow of a different
person who is facing neglect? Can you join his dreams? The man’s answer is not a condemnation,
but the sorrow of not having a group that understands him and holds him together. Our mission is
to become that group which understand and hold together.

St. Matt. 7: 21-27
Whenever a builder starts constructing a house, the most important work happens where
no one can see. Before the walls go up, and long before the paint dries, the builder has to dig down
deep into the dirt until they strike solid rock. If they take shortcuts and ignore the foundation, even
the most beautiful house will come crashing down the moment a heavy storm hits.
Today, on this Youth Sunday, we live in a world that focuses almost entirely on the outside.
We are constantly taught to look successful, keep our social media feeds bright, and pretend that
our lives are completely put together. But behind those bright smiles, many of our youth are quietly
struggling. There is the heavy stress of exams, the search for stable jobs, the ache of loneliness
in distant cities and hostels, and the fear of falling behind. In Matthew 7, Jesus does not care about
the paint on our walls. He looks straight through the appearance and asks one vital question: what
is holding your life up from beneath?
1.  Rooted in Christ: Going Beyond the Surface
Jesus warns us that simply saying “Lord, Lord” is never enough. It is easy to come to
church every Sunday, wear nice clothes, sing the songs, and still be building our lives on loose
sand. Sand is comfortable because it requires zero effort. It means living for instant likes, following
the crowd, and treating God like an afterthought.
Building on the rock takes real work. It means choosing to dig past our pride and our selfish
desires. To be rooted in Christ means our worth is not decided by our job title, our salary, or what
people say about us. It means making time every day to pray, read His Word, and anchor our
identity in the love of Jesus. When your roots grip the bedrock of Christ, no trend or hardship can
wash you away.
2. Driven by Faith: Hearing That Becomes Doing
Both builders in the parable heard the exact same words of Jesus. The only difference was
that one walked away and did nothing, while the other went home and put those words into practice.
Real faith is never just sitting quietly in a pew. Faith has hands and feet.
In our Mar Thoma tradition, faith is always meant to be lived out. When we are driven by
faith, our belief changes how we act on Monday morning. It means being honest in an office where
others cheat. It means standing up for a friend who is left out. It means trusting God with your
future even when the doors seem closed. Faith does not keep the rain away, but it gives us the
courage to keep walking through the downpour.
This question remains before us as followers of Christ. Can you join the sorrow of a different
person who is facing neglect? Can you join his dreams? The man’s answer is not a condemnation,
but the sorrow of not having a group that understands him and holds him together. Our mission is
to become that group which understand and hold together.

Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have become an essential infrastructure for Artificial General
Intelligence (AGI), yet their lack of well-defined memory management systems hinders the devel-
opment of long-context reasoning, continual personalization, and knowledge consistency.Existing
models mainly rely on static parameters and short-lived contextual states, limiting their ability to
track user preferences or update knowledge over extended periods.While Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG) introduces external knowledge in plain text, it remains a stateless workaround
without lifecycle control or integration with persistent representations.Recent work has modeled the
training and inference cost of LLMs from a memory hierarchy perspective, showing that introducing
an explicit memory layer between parameter memory and external retrieval can substantially
reduce these costs by externalizing specific knowledge [1]. Beyond computational efficiency, LLMs
face broader challenges arising from how information is distributed over time and context, requiring
systems capable of managing heterogeneous knowledge spanning different temporal scales and
sources. To address this challenge, we propose MemOS, a memory operating system that treats
memory as a manageable system resource. It unifies the representation, scheduling, and evolution
of plaintext, activation-based, and parameter-level memories, enabling cost-efficient storage and
retrieval. As the basic unit, a MemCube encapsulates both memory content and metadata such as
provenance and versioning. MemCubes can be composed, migrated, and fused over time, enabling
flexible transitions between memory types and bridging retrieval with parameter-based learning.
MemOS establishes a memory-centric system framework that brings controllability, plasticity, and
evolvability to LLMs, laying the foundation for continual learning and personalized modeling.

flexible transitions between memory types and bridging retrieval with parameter-based learning.
MemOS establishes a memory-centric system framework that brings controllability, plasticity, and
evolvability to LLMs, laying the foundation for continual learning and personalized modeling.

Module 3 – Project Management, Software 
Development & IT Operations 
1. Scope, Time and Cost — Triple Constraints 
The Triple Constraint is a framework used in project management to balance three major 
factors: 
Scope + Time + Cost 
• Scope – What the project must deliver: features, work and deliverables. 
• Time – How long the project will take. 
• Cost – The budget and resources needed, including people, technology and other 
expenses. 
These three are interconnected. Changing one usually affects the other two. 
Example 
Suppose a college is developing an online examination system. 
Initial scope: 
• Student login 
• Online examination 
• Result generation 
• Basic reports 
Planned: 
• Time: 6 months 
• Cost: ₹10 lakh 
Later, the college asks for: 
• Mobile application 
• Biometric authentication 
• Video proctoring

Module 2 — IT Governance and Standards 
1. Internal IT Controls 
Internal IT controls are policies, procedures, processes and technical measures used to protect 
assets, ensure correct operations, comply with regulations and reduce security risks. An IT audit 
checks whether these controls are properly designed, implemented and working. 
Types of controls 
Type 
Purpose 
Example 
Preventive 
Stop incidents before they happen 
MFA, firewall, strong passwords 
Detective 
Detect incidents after they occur 
Logs, IDS, audit trails 
Corrective 
Recover/reduce damage 
Backups, disaster recovery, patching 
Real-life example: 
A college LMS uses MFA to prevent unauthorized login → preventive. It keeps login logs to 
detect suspicious activity → detective. It uses backups after a ransomware attack → corrective. 
Main objectives 
Protect information, prevent unauthorized access, maintain CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, 
Availability), detect/respond to incidents, meet legal requirements and reduce risks. 
 
2. Framework vs Standard 
Framework 
A flexible roadmap that tells an organization how to approach security/governance. 
Standard 
A specific set of requirements/rules that an organization should follow.

1. Introduction and Purpose
·
MTYS was established in 1933 and has completed 93 years of ministry.
·
Its main purpose is to help young people accept Jesus Christ as Lord, God and Saviour.
·
Its four pillars are Worship, Study, Witness and Service.
2. Organisation and Leadership
·
MTYS has 785 registered Sakhas across the Mar Thoma Church.
·
It is led by a 66-member Managing Committee.
·
It has 8 full-time workers serving in its various offices and centres.
3. Social Service – MYSDA
·
Society for Development Actions (MYSDA) is a dedicated organization which works for
social development.

·
Parish youth programmes, camps and conferences.
·
50-day Lenten worship and meditation programme.
·
Bible studies, literary competitions and study book examinations.
·
Anti-drug awareness programmes in schools and colleges.
·
Environmental protection activities.
·
Intensive Training Institute (ITI) to develop interest in evangelism and mission work.
·
Youth programmes at the Maramon Convention.
5. Mar Thoma Youth Centre, Adoor
·
A major camp and conference centre in Central Travancore.
·
Has an 800-seat auditorium and accommodation for 400 people.
·
Hosts church conferences, camps and other gatherings.
6. Outside-Kerala Office and Youth Centre
·
Located in Bangalore.
·
Coordinates MTYS activities in dioceses outside Kerala.
7. Sakhyam Gramam – Kadapa Mission
·
A mission project launched during the 80th anniversary of MTYS.
·
Aims to strengthen mission activities according to local needs.
